prompt: A resource is valuable and rare, but competitors can imitate it at low cost. According to VRIO, what does it provide?

options.text: Temporary competitive advantage
Competitive parity
Sustained competitive advantage
Competitive disadvantage

explanation: Not valuable → disadvantage; valuable but not rare → parity; valuable and rare but imitable → temporary advantage; V+R+I+O → sustained advantage.

prompt: Which are capabilities rather than resources? Select all that apply.

options.text: Using client data to improve the production process
Managing cash flows
Skilled employees
A portfolio of patents

explanation: Resources = what we have (nouns): client data, cash, skilled employees, patents. Capabilities = what we do (verbs): using data, managing cash flows, motivating and training employees.

prompt: Which are sources of inimitability mentioned in class? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ambiguity about how resources are linked together (the “recipe”)
Culture and history, tacit knowledge
The resource can be bought easily on factor markets
Costly substitution (in VRIO, substitution is folded into I)

explanation: Causal ambiguity, culture/history and tacit knowledge make imitation costly. A resource that can be bought easily is mobile and therefore imitable.

prompt: Which assumptions distinguish the resource-based view from environmental models of competitive advantage? Select all that apply.

options.text: Firms in an industry may be heterogeneous in the strategic resources they control
Resources may be imperfectly mobile, so heterogeneity can last
Industry structure explains most of a firm's performance
Resources can always be bought and sold on factor markets

explanation: Environmental (IO) models implicitly assume homogeneous and mobile resources. RBV (Barney 1991) assumes heterogeneity and imperfect mobility.

prompt: Which of the following are primary activities in Porter's value chain? Select all that apply.

options.text: Inbound logistics
Marketing & sales
Service
Technology development
Procurement

explanation: Primary: inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, marketing & sales, service. Support: procurement, technology development, HRM, firm infrastructure.

prompt: In VRIO, what does the “O” question ask?

options.text: Is the organization appropriately organized (processes, structure, control, incentives) to exploit the resource?
Is the resource owned rather than rented?
Is the resource used in operations?
Is the resource oriented towards new markets?

explanation: O = organizational support, a complementary capability. V, R and I describe the resource; O describes the organization (Barney 1995).

prompt: In the Dyson case, which statement reflects the course's lesson about entering electric vehicles?

options.text: A resource may be VRIO in one industry but not in another
Because Dyson's brand is VRIO in vacuums, it automatically gives a sustained advantage in cars
Funding is Dyson's most inimitable resource
VRIO cannot be used to evaluate entry into a new industry

explanation: Dyson's experience and innovation culture were less rare/inimitable against Tesla, BYD or BMW. VRIO helps decide whether to enter – Dyson abandoned the EV project in 2019.

prompt: Which statements on SWOT are correct according to the course? Select all that apply.

options.text: Strengths and weaknesses are internal and actual
Opportunities and threats are external and potential
Factors should be weighted and prioritized
A SWOT can replace a detailed industry and resource analysis

explanation: SWOT is a simple heuristic; without prior analysis the perception of the real SWOTs is biased.

prompt: Basic video game hardware with sufficient technical specifications is, for a console maker, an example of…

options.text: a threshold resource/capability
a distinctive capability
a dynamic capability
an intangible resource

explanation: Threshold resources are needed to compete at parity (Nintendo case); distinctive ones create advantage. Both change as industries evolve.

statement: According to the RBV, the competitive advantage of a firm is explained mainly by its position in an attractive industry.
explanation: That is the top-down IO view. RBV is bottom-up: distinctive resources and capabilities explain superior performance.

statement: In VRIO, the customers or stakeholders – not the producers – qualify a resource as valuable.
explanation: Value is not an absolute attribute of a product or service.

statement: Rarity in VRIO is an absolute concept: a resource is rare only if no other firm in the world has it.
explanation: Rare = possessed by one or a few organizations; competitive advantage is about relative, not absolute performance.

statement: Brand reputation and intellectual property are intangible resources.
explanation: Tangible: capital, land, buildings, plant, equipment, supplies. Intangible: culture, knowledge, brand & reputation, IP.

statement: In the move from VRIN to VRIO, non-substitutability was dropped entirely from the analysis.
explanation: It was folded into I: is the resource costly to imitate OR substitute? O was added.

statement: Support activities in the value chain add value indirectly by supporting primary activities.
explanation: Procurement, technology development, HRM, firm infrastructure.

statement: Dynamic capabilities are needed because VRIO assumes relatively stable industries, while industries change over the long term.
explanation: Teece: renew and recreate resources and capabilities to meet changing environments.

statement: Threshold and distinctive resources stay the same over the life of an industry.
explanation: Both change as industries change, and it is hard to predict future threshold and distinctive resources.

statement: The value system includes the value chains of suppliers, the organization and its customers.
explanation: A single organization rarely performs all activities from design to delivery; analysing the value system supports make-or-buy decisions.

prompt: Using a VRIO analysis, assess whether Dyson's patent portfolio and its engineering team provide a sustained competitive advantage in vacuum cleaners.
modelAnswer: Patent portfolio (robots, cameras, AI, aerodynamics, motors): valuable – protects the bagless cyclone and digital motor technologies customers pay a premium for; rare – unique technologies; inimitable – legally protected, Dyson aggressively litigates (Hoover paid damages); organized – Dyson invests heavily in R&D and defends IP, and its direct sales and stores exploit the technology → sustained competitive advantage (until patents expire, which is why continuous innovation matters). Engineering team (UK, Singapore, China): valuable and rare (scarce engineers, Dyson Institute) but imitable – rivals can hire engineers, and non-competes are limited → temporary competitive advantage on its own.
keyPoints: Patents: V, R, I, O each argued with case facts
Engineers: V and R but imitable

prompt: Explain the difference between resources and capabilities, and between threshold and distinctive resources. Give an example for each.
modelAnswer: Resources are the assets an organization has or can call upon (nouns), e.g. client data, cash, skilled employees, a brand. Capabilities are the ways these assets are deployed (verbs), e.g. using client data to improve production, managing cash flows, training employees. Threshold resources and capabilities are those needed to compete at all and achieve parity, e.g. adequate technical specifications for a game console or a booking website for a hotel. Distinctive resources and capabilities are superior and create competitive advantage, e.g. Dyson's digital motor know-how or Nintendo's ability to design new forms of play. What is threshold or distinctive changes as the industry evolves.

prompt: Why do firms need dynamic capabilities? Illustrate with an example.
modelAnswer: VRIO resources can produce a sustained advantage, but only if industries and markets stay stable. Over the long term, environments change: resources get imitated, become common practice or redundant. Dynamic capabilities (Teece) are the ability to create, extend or modify the firm's resources and capabilities to meet changing environments. Example: Nintendo repeatedly reinvented its offering (Game Boy, DS, Wii, Switch, mobile games) when technology and customers changed; Dyson extended motor and airflow know-how from vacuums to hair dryers and air purifiers; VfB Stuttgart built a repeatable scouting and development process that survives the sale of its best players.
keyPoints: Definition of dynamic capabilities (create, extend, modify)
